unit.title: Develop an understanding of business operations

summary: This unit helps you understand how a hotel or villa works as a business: what a business is and why tourism matters to Jamaica, the types of business ownership, how departments are organised and work together, how money comes in and goes out, how stock and costs are controlled, how a property finds its guests, and how your own work affects the business.

blocks.p: A hotel or villa is a business. It has to give guests a good stay and also earn enough money to pay its staff, its bills and its owners. Workers who understand this make better decisions: they waste less, they take more care with guests, and they see why their jobs matter.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. You do not need to be a manager to understand business operations. A room attendant who cleans a room properly, switches off the air conditioning in an empty room and treats guests well is helping the business make a profit.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper with multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, and two group practical tasks. In the first you draw an organisation chart for a 40-room hotel and make a guest journey poster showing how departments work together. In the second you plan and cost a villa weekend package for 6 guests, work out a selling price, do a SWOT, and design a promotion. Work every sum twice.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Use only made-up names, costs and pictures in your practical. Never use real guests' photos or details.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What a business is, and tourism in Jamaica

blocks.p: A **business** is an organisation that provides goods or services to customers, usually to make a profit. **Goods** are things you can touch, such as a bag of coffee or a souvenir T-shirt. **Services** are things done for you, such as a laundry service, an airport transfer or a meal served at your table.

Hotels and villas sell mainly services (rooms, meals, tours, transfers) and some goods (gift shop items, bottles of drink). Tourism and hospitality are part of the **service industry**. In a service business, the way people are treated is part of what is sold.

The main aim of most hotels and villas is to give guests good service and to make a **profit**: money left after the costs are paid. Without profit, a business cannot pay wages, repair buildings or grow.

ul: **Foreign exchange**: visitors spend US dollars and other currencies, which the country uses to pay for imports such as fuel, food and machinery.
**Jobs**: directly in hotels, villas, attractions and transport; indirectly for farmers, fishers, craft makers, taxi operators, entertainers and suppliers.
**Taxes**: tourism businesses and visitors pay taxes, which help to pay for roads, schools and health care.
**Development**: airports, roads and services that local people use too.

blocks.h: How a villa can support its community

ul: Buy fresh fruit, vegetables and fish from local farmers and fishers: this supports the local economy and keeps food fresh. Check quality on delivery, as you would for any supplier.
Use local tradespeople for repairs, and recommend local guides, restaurants and craft markets to guests.
Hire and train people from the area.
Protect the environment: save water and energy, and dispose of waste properly.
Take part in community projects. When local people benefit, they welcome visitors, and the whole industry gains.

blocks.note: Tourism depends on good weather, safety, a good name and happy guests. Events such as hurricanes, crime, disease or a bad reputation can reduce visitor numbers quickly, which is why a business must plan ahead.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Types of business, planning and registering

head: Type
Who owns it
Advantage
Disadvantage
rows: One person, who runs it and keeps all the profit
Easy and cheap to set up; full control
Carries all the risk; her own savings and property may be lost if the business fails; limited money and skills
Two or more people who share work, money and profit
More skills and money; shared work
Disagreements; partners may be responsible for each other's debts
Shareholders; the company is a separate legal body
Owners' own money is protected if it fails; easier to raise money
More records, rules and reports; costs more to set up
Its members, who share the profit and have an equal say
Shared work and risk; fair sharing; good for small producers (craft vendors, farmers)
Decisions can be slow; members must agree

blocks.p: Example: two cousins who run a guest house together and share the profit, without forming a company, are a **partnership**.

ul: A **business plan** is a written plan that sets goals, describes the product and market, estimates costs and income, and shows how the business will make a profit. Owners write one to think things through and to win support or a loan.

A **mission statement** is a short statement of the business's main purpose, such as 'to give every guest a warm Jamaican welcome and a clean, comfortable stay'. It guides decisions and tells staff and guests what the business stands for.

A new business must be **registered** and must get the **licences and permits** it needs: for example, registering the business name or company, getting a Taxpayer Registration Number, and the approvals for tourism accommodation, food service and fire and health safety. Ask the relevant offices which ones apply. Open first and register later is not an option.
Know how much money you need to start, where it will come from (savings, a loan, a partner), and when you expect to make a profit.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, many villas are owned by individuals or families and managed by a villa manager or a management company. Always ask who owns the property and who you report to.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: How a hotel or villa is organised

head: Department
What it does
rows: Takes reservations, checks guests in and out, handles guest bills and payments, answers questions. It is the centre of communication.
Cleans and prepares guest rooms and public areas, looks after linen and laundry, reports maintenance problems and lost property.
Serves meals and drinks in the restaurant, bar, room service and at events. The kitchen plans menus and prepares the food.
Keeps the building, air conditioning, plumbing, electrics, pool pumps and grounds in good working order.
Protects guests, staff and property, and controls who comes in.
Promotes the property, makes deals with travel companies and brings in bookings and events.
Handles the money: guest bills, payments to suppliers, payroll and records.
Recruits, trains and looks after the staff, and keeps staff records.

blocks.p: A villa has fewer staff, so one person may do several jobs. The **villa manager** may handle bookings, accounts and guests, while a **housekeeper**, **cook**, **butler**, **gardener**, **pool attendant** and **security guard** look after the guests and the property. The butler looks after guests' personal needs and serves meals and drinks.
An **organisation chart** is a diagram that shows the departments and jobs and who reports to whom.

head: Level
Example jobs in housekeeping
rows: Room attendants, public area attendants, laundry attendants

ul: A **reporting line** shows who your supervisor is. Room attendants report to a supervisor or the executive housekeeper, not to the chefs or the front desk.
If you have a problem with your work schedule, speak to **your supervisor** first, then up the line if needed.
A guest complaint goes to the supervisor of the department concerned.

head: System
What it does
rows: Reservations, check-in, room status and guest bills at the front office
The till system in the bar and restaurant; sends charges to the guest's bill
Booking engine and online travel sites

blocks.p: The PMS handles bookings, check-in and bills. It does not control the pool pumps or the kitchen.
A guest sees one business. Each department depends on the others, so information must be passed on. Here is how one guest's stay passes through the departments.

head: Stage
Who does what
Information passed on
rows: Reservations (front office) record the dates, room type and special requests
Late arrival, a food allergy, a baby cot: sent to housekeeping and the kitchen
Front office tells housekeeping which rooms are needed. Housekeeping cleans and checks them
Housekeeping reports to the front office as soon as each room is ready, so the room can be given to an arriving guest
Front office checks the guest in; bell staff take bags
Key and room number; any special requests
Restaurant and bar serve; housekeeping cleans; maintenance repairs
A broken air conditioner is logged by the front office and sent to maintenance, then checked with the guest
Front office settles the bill; accounts records the payment
Housekeeping is told the room is empty

ul: Use phones, radios, a log book and written handovers. Do not leave messages by word of mouth only.
Help other departments at busy times, and respect their work.
If one department lets another down, the guest suffers. A kitchen that is not told about an allergy cannot protect the guest.

blocks.p: A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a written, step-by-step way of doing a task, such as making a bed or checking in a guest. Written procedures mean every guest gets the same good standard, whoever is on duty. They also make it easier to train new staff and to see what went wrong.

ul: Follow the procedure, and suggest improvements to your supervisor.
Guest feedback forms and comment cards show what to improve and what works.
Quality is checked by supervisors' inspections, guest comments and online reviews.
Satisfied guests come back, recommend the property and write good online reviews. This brings new guests at little cost.
Satisfied guests spend more on extras such as meals, tours and spa treatments.
**Repeat guests** cost less to win than new guests and bring steady income. They often recommend the property.
Poor service brings complaints, refunds, bad reviews and fewer bookings. Future guests read reviews before they book.

blocks.p: Know your guests. Business guests need quick check-in, fast Wi-Fi and wake-up calls. Families need a cot, a high chair and a safe pool. Honeymooners want privacy and romance. Ask what each guest needs.

Other properties are your **competitors**. A **competitive advantage** is something your property does better than the others: a warm welcome, a private chef, a better view, cleaner rooms, lower prices in the low season, or a location close to the beach. Find what makes your property special and build on it.
A **SWOT** analysis is a simple way to look at a business and plan ahead. **Strengths** and **weaknesses** are inside the business. **Opportunities** and **threats** come from outside it.

head: Box
Example for a small villa near Negril
rows: Beach view; a cook who makes excellent Jamaican food; many good online reviews
An old website; only three bedrooms; no staff who speak Spanish or French
A new direct flight bringing more visitors; more interest in beach weddings; local visitors on public holidays
A hurricane forecast; a large new hotel nearby with lower prices; rising electricity costs

blocks.p: After the SWOT, the owner plans: build on the strengths, fix the weaknesses (a new website), take up the opportunities (a wedding package) and prepare for the threats (insurance and a hurricane plan). Review a SWOT every year.

head: Term
Meaning
Examples
rows: All the money the business receives
Room sales, meals, drinks, tours, laundry, transfers
Money the business spends to operate
Wages, food and drink, electricity, water, linen, cleaning supplies, repairs, rent, insurance
J$900 000 income - J$650 000 expenses = J$250 000 profit
J$500 000 income - J$560 000 expenses = a loss of J$60 000

head: Type
Meaning
Examples
rows: Stay about the same however many guests come
Rent, insurance, manager's salary, loan repayments
Go up when more guests are served
Food and drink, laundry, cleaning products, guest soaps, some electricity

blocks.p: In the low season, income falls but fixed costs do not. A business must plan for this, for example by saving in the high season.

ul: A **budget** is a plan of the income and spending expected over a set period, such as a year. A department such as housekeeping plans how much it will spend on linen and supplies, to control spending and to avoid running short of money.

**Cash flow** is the money coming in and going out over time. A business can make a profit and still run out of cash, for example if guests pay late but suppliers and wages must be paid on time. Watch the timing, and keep a reserve.
Keep records of all income and expenses. They show whether the business is making a profit.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Example
rows: J$150 000 room income from 10 rooms sold: J$150 000 ÷ 10 = J$15 000

ul: The **high season** in Jamaica is roughly December to April, when many visitors come to escape the northern winter. Demand and rates are highest, and more staff and stock are needed.

The **low season** is roughly late spring to autumn, and includes the hurricane season (June to November). Fewer guests come. To attract guests, properties lower rates, offer packages and target local and regional guests, and use quiet times for repairs, deep cleaning and training.
Plan rosters so that staff hours match the work: more in busy times, fewer in quiet times.

head: Plan
What the rate includes
rows: CP or BP (Continental or Bermuda Plan)
Room, breakfast and one main meal, usually dinner
Room, all meals, drinks and many activities

blocks.p: Properties may use slightly different names. Always check what the rate includes and tell the guest clearly.

blocks.h: Costing a package: a worked example

blocks.p: A villa plans a weekend package for 6 guests. The costs are: food and drink J$4 000 per guest; airport transfers J$12 000 in total; a river tour J$3 500 per guest; extra staff hours J$15 000; and the villa's share of fixed costs (electricity, insurance) J$18 000. The target profit is J$30 000.

blocks.note: If the villa charges only the cost per guest (J$15 000), it makes no profit: it only breaks even. If GCT applies to the villa, show the price as 'plus GCT at the current rate' and never as a figure you have not checked. Ask someone else to check every sum.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **GCT** (General Consumption Tax) is added to many prices and bills at the current rate. It is collected for the government and is not the property's income. If a guest asks why the bill is more than the menu prices, tax and any service charge are the likely reasons.
Stock control makes sure a villa has what it needs when it needs it, without waste or theft. **Stock** includes food, drinks, linen, cleaning supplies and guest amenities.

flow: Set a par level for each item
Order what is below par, from approved suppliers, in writing

ul: A **par level** is the amount that should always be in stock, for example enough sets of linen for every bed, and toilet rolls for a week. It stops running short and stops overbuying.
A **supplier** is a business that sells goods, such as food or linen, to the property.

**Receiving a delivery**: check it against the order and the invoice for quantity, quality, dates and temperature. Chilled food should arrive cold (5 °C or below) and frozen food frozen. **Refuse** or report anything warm, damaged, out of date or short, and record the problem.
**Storage**: dry goods off the floor in a clean, dry store; chilled food at 5 °C or below; chemicals apart from food and linen. Use the oldest stock first: **first in, first out (FIFO)**.
**Security**: lock stores, sign items out, keep records, and report damage, spoilage or missing items at once.

blocks.h: How staff help to control costs

head: Cost
What you can do
rows: Follow recipes and portion sizes; cut waste; store food properly; use older stock first
Switch off lights and air conditioning in empty rooms; keep fridge doors shut
Report dripping taps and leaks at once; do not leave taps running
Use the correct dilution; do not overuse chemicals
Handle with care; report damage; do not use towels as cleaning cloths
Record every drink and meal, including staff and friends; never take items without permission

blocks.note: Giving free drinks to friends without recording them is theft. It reduces the bar's profit and can cost you your job and your reputation.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Every worker's actions affect the profit. A room attendant whose rooms are clean and ready helps the hotel sell them and get repeat guests. A careless one costs the business money.
**Marketing** is how a hotel or villa finds guests and persuades them to book. It is more than advertising.

head: Part of marketing
What it means for a villa
rows: What you sell, and what makes it special: a sea view, a private chef, a quiet location
The group of customers you mainly aim to sell to: couples, families, friends, wedding groups
Set to suit the market and the season; lower in the low season
Where guests can book: your own website, online travel websites, travel agents and tour operators, phone and email
Telling people: good photos and videos, social media, special offers, advertising, travel fairs

ul: **Online travel websites** usually charge the property a **commission** on each booking. Encouraging repeat guests to book directly saves commission.
**Online reviews** are very important: encourage happy guests to write them and reply politely to every review.
Offer repeat guests a welcome-back gift or discount, and keep in touch with a newsletter.
Posting photos and offers on social media is a form of promotion. Do not use guests' photos without permission.
Staff are part of marketing, too: every friendly greeting and well-cleaned room makes guests more likely to recommend the property.

blocks.note: An honest promotion shows the real price (and says plus GCT if that applies), real photos and what is included. A guest who arrives to find less than was promised writes a bad review.
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: Two sisters plan a guest house in Port Antonio
c1.text: Sisters Marcia and Janet Francis want to open a small guest house with six bedrooms in Port Antonio. They plan to use their savings and a loan, and they will do the cooking and cleaning themselves at first. They have not yet written a business plan or registered anything. They plan to be open before the busy season starts.

c2.title: Costing a weekend package
c2.text: A villa plans a weekend package for 6 guests. The costs are: food and drink J$4 000 per guest; airport transfers J$12 000 in total; a river tour J$3 500 per guest; extra staff hours J$15 000; and the villa's share of fixed costs J$18 000. The villa wants a profit of J$30 000 on the package. The villa is registered for GCT.

c3.title: A quiet September at a hotel in Negril
c3.text: A 16-room hotel in Negril sells 10 rooms on a night in September, which is in the low season and the hurricane season. Its room income for the night is J$150 000. The owner worries that the hotel's loan payments, insurance and managers' salaries stay the same every month, while fewer guests are booking.

c4.title: Stock problems at a villa in Montego Bay
c4.text: A villa in Montego Bay has three problems in one week. A delivery of frozen fish arrives with ice crystals and the box is soft, as if it has partly thawed. The linen count shows ten towels fewer than the par level. And the cook finds that the oldest tins of tomatoes are at the back of the store, behind newly delivered stock.

c5.title: Marketing a villa in Port Antonio
c5.text: A three-bedroom villa in Port Antonio gets most of its bookings through an online travel website, which charges a commission on each booking. The owner, Mrs Campbell, wants to attract couples on honeymoon and to keep guests coming back. The villa has a beautiful view and a cook who is known for her Jamaican food, but only one member of staff speaks Spanish.

questions.q: If only Marcia had opened the guest house, as a sole trader, which risk would she carry herself?
o: If the business failed, her own savings and property could be lost
She would have to share every decision with a group of members who have an equal vote
She would have to publish accounts, as a separate company with shareholders must do
She would have to split the profit with the bank, which lent the money for the beds
questions.why: A sole trader keeps all the profit but also carries all the risk, and her own savings and property are not protected if the business fails. Equal votes belong to a co-operative; separate accounts and shareholders belong to a limited company.

questions.q: What is one risk of a partnership for the sisters?
o: They may disagree, and each may be responsible for the business's debts
The business must publish its accounts every year, so that anyone can read them
The business can only have one owner and may not hire any other people to work for it
The owners' homes and savings are completely protected if the business fails
questions.why: Partners can disagree, and in a simple partnership each partner can be responsible for the business's debts. Protection of the owners' own money is an advantage of a limited company.

questions.q: Why should the sisters write a business plan?
o: To set goals, check costs and income, and show how they will make a profit
To give to every guest who books, so that they know the prices before arrival
To avoid needing licences or registration, since the plan shows their intentions
To list the staff uniforms and the rules for the guests of the guest house
questions.why: A business plan sets goals, estimates costs and income, shows how profit will come and can be used to win a loan. It does not replace registration or licences.

questions.q: Which step is part of setting up the guest house legally?
o: Register the business and get the licences and permits it needs first
Open and welcome guests first, and register after the first season has passed
Ask the guests to register the business as soon as they have booked rooms
Print menus, price lists and brochures, since these are what the law requires
questions.why: A business must be registered and have the permits it needs before it opens. Opening first and registering later can lead to fines or closure.

questions.q: What is the total cost of the weekend package for 6 guests?
What is the cost per guest?
questions.why: Total cost J$90 000 divided by 6 guests = J$15 000. This is the price at which the villa only breaks even.

questions.q: What selling price per guest meets the target profit of J$30 000 (before GCT)?
questions.why: Income needed = cost J$90 000 + profit J$30 000 = J$120 000. Divided by 6 guests = J$20 000 each.

questions.q: Which of the costs on the card is a variable cost?
o: Food and drink for each guest
The villa's share of fixed costs
The extra staff hours for the weekend
The airport transfers for the group
questions.why: A variable cost goes up when more guests are served, such as food and drink per guest. The share of fixed costs is fixed by definition. The other two are set for the whole package.

questions.q: How should the promotion show the price, as the villa is registered for GCT?
o: J$20 000 per guest, plus GCT at the current rate
J$20 000 per guest, with no mention of tax anywhere on the flyer
J$20 000 per guest, with a GCT figure copied from a flyer of another villa
J$15 000 per guest, since the villa must pay GCT out of its own profit
questions.why: An honest promotion shows the price and says plus GCT at the current rate. Hiding the tax annoys guests at check-out, and using a figure from somewhere else may be wrong.

questions.q: What is the hotel's occupancy for the night?
questions.why: Occupancy = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100 = 10 ÷ 16 × 100 = 62.5%.

questions.q: In the high season the hotel sells all 16 rooms for the night at an average of J$15 000 each. What is its room income for that night?
questions.why: Room income = rooms sold × average rate = 16 × J$15 000 = J$240 000. J$150 000 was the September income from 10 rooms.

questions.q: Why is the owner worried about the loan payments, insurance and salaries in the low season?
o: They are fixed costs, which stay the same even when income falls
They are variable costs, which rise when fewer guests come to the hotel
They are income, which is lower whenever the hurricane season begins
They are profit, which the owner must share with the staff and the bank
questions.why: Fixed costs do not change with guest numbers. In the low season, income falls but these costs continue, so the hotel must plan, save in the high season and look for other business.

questions.q: The driver of the fish delivery says the fish is fine and asks the clerk to sign quickly because he is late. What should the clerk do before signing?
o: Check the delivery against the order and invoice, and check the temperature
Sign first, then check the box when the driver has left, in case there are any problems
Ask the cook to taste a piece of the fish, and sign if it seems fresh enough to him
Sign for it and note the problem on the invoice, so the cook can decide what to do later
questions.why: A delivery must be checked before it is signed for: quantity, quality, dates and temperature against the order and invoice. Once you sign, the business accepts the goods.

questions.q: Ten towels are missing against the par level. What is the best first step?
o: Check the laundry and the rooms, record the shortage, and report it
Order twenty more towels at once and say nothing about the missing ones
Assume that guests took them, and add a charge to every guest's bill
Cut the par level by ten, so that the count is correct on paper again
questions.why: Find out where the towels are (laundry, rooms, store), record the shortage and report it, so the cause can be found. Charging guests or changing the par level hides the problem.

questions.q: The oldest tins of tomatoes are at the back, behind new stock. What should the cook do?
o: Move the older tins to the front, and use the oldest stock first
Leave them where they are, since the new tins are easier to reach
Use the new tins first, to keep the old ones for an emergency
Throw away all the older tins, whether they are still in date or not
questions.why: First in, first out means older stock is used first, so that food does not go out of date and waste money. Store new stock behind older stock.

questions.q: The towel par level is 60 sets, and today's count finds 48 sets in total. What should be done?
o: Order the 12 sets that are short from an approved supplier, in writing
Do nothing, since 48 sets are enough while the villa is not full of guests
Lower the par level to 48, so that the count and the par level agree
Order 60 more sets, so that the stock cannot ever fall below the par level
questions.why: A par level is the stock that should always be held. A count below par means reordering the difference, from approved suppliers, in writing. Changing the par level to match the count hides the shortage.

questions.q: How could Mrs Campbell reduce the commission she pays the online travel website?
o: Encourage repeat guests to book directly with the villa
Ask the website to charge guests the commission instead of the villa
Stop answering reviews, so that the website cannot count the bookings
Raise the villa's rates in the low season so that the commission is a smaller part
questions.why: Direct bookings, especially from happy repeat guests, do not carry a commission. Good service, a welcome-back offer and keeping in touch with guests help.

questions.q: Who is the 'target market' Mrs Campbell is aiming at?
o: Couples on honeymoon, the group she mainly wants to sell to
Every visitor who has ever stayed in a villa anywhere in Jamaica
Other villa owners, who might pass bookings on to her for a fee
The staff of the online travel website that sends her the bookings
questions.why: A target market is the group of customers a business mainly aims to sell to. Knowing it lets the villa choose suitable prices, photos, packages and promotion.

questions.q: In a SWOT for the villa, the Spanish-speaking staff member is only one person. Where does this belong?
o: Weakness: it is inside the business and may limit service to guests
Threat: it comes from outside the business and may cost the villa guests
Opportunity: it comes from outside and will bring more Spanish-speaking guests
Strength: with only one speaker, the villa always has someone for Spanish guests
questions.why: Weaknesses are inside the business. The villa could fix it by training more staff. Opportunities and threats come from outside, such as a new flight or a hurricane.

questions.q: A villa made a profit last year, but cannot pay its electricity bill in September because several guests have not paid yet. What does this show?
o: A cash flow problem: money coming in later than the bills must be paid
A loss: the villa's expenses were more than its income for the whole year
An occupancy problem: too few rooms were sold in the high season last year
A marketing problem: the villa needs to advertise more in the autumn months
questions.why: Cash flow is the timing of money coming in and going out. A business can be profitable over the year and still run short of cash when payments arrive late, so it needs a reserve and careful watch on payments.
